questions.scenario: Downstream code parses the model reply and fails when a field name changes between calls.
questions.question: Which feature should you use?

options.text: A higher temperature
options.why: It makes variation more likely.

options.text: A longer system message that asks nicely for JSON
options.why: Instructions alone do not guarantee the schema.

options.text: Streaming the response
options.why: Streaming changes delivery, not structure.

options.text: Structured outputs with a strict JSON schema
options.why: Correct. The reply must match the schema.

questions.explanation: Structured outputs constrain the model to your schema. JSON mode only promises valid JSON.

questions.scenario: A claims flow calls a warranty system that sometimes times out. The flow must never send a reply that lacks verified data.
questions.question: What should you implement?

options.text: A limited number of retries, then a fallback that holds the claim for a person
options.why: Correct. The flow stays safe when the tool fails.

options.text: Let the model guess the warranty status when the tool fails
options.why: A guess can produce a wrong promise to the customer.

options.text: Remove the tool and rely on the prompt
options.why: The data is only available from the system.

options.text: Retry forever until the tool responds
options.why: Unlimited retries can hang the flow.

questions.explanation: Plan for failure in code: bounded retries, a safe fallback and a check before sending.

questions.scenario: A single prompt classifies a claim, extracts fields, checks the warranty and writes the reply. Failures are hard to diagnose.
questions.question: What is the best redesign?

options.text: Move all steps into the system message
options.why: It keeps one combined prompt.

options.text: Split the work into steps, each with a focused prompt and a check between steps
options.why: Correct. Each step can be tested and traced on its own.

options.text: Add more text to the single prompt
options.why: A longer prompt makes failures harder to isolate.

options.text: Use a higher temperature
options.why: It does not improve diagnosability.

questions.explanation: Multistep pipelines give one job per step, with validation in between.

questions.question: Which setting is most appropriate for the classification step of a flow that must give the same label for the same email?

options.text: A max output tokens value of 1,000
options.why: Output length does not make the label consistent.

options.text: A larger context window
options.why: A bigger window does not make output repeatable.

options.text: Temperature 0
options.why: Correct. It gives the most repeatable output.

options.text: Temperature 1.5
options.why: A high temperature adds variation.

questions.explanation: Use low temperature for classification and extraction, where consistency matters.

questions.scenario: You are designing a reasoning pipeline that has several model calls and one external tool call.
questions.question: Which two practices improve reliability? Select two.

options.text: Set timeouts and a maximum number of retries on the tool call
options.why: Correct. Bounds keep the pipeline predictable.

options.text: Pass every earlier message to every step regardless of need
options.why: Extra context adds cost and can confuse later steps.

options.text: Use the highest temperature for extraction steps
options.why: High temperature reduces repeatability.

options.text: Validate each step output before it becomes the next step input
options.why: Correct. Early validation stops errors spreading.

questions.explanation: Checks between steps and bounds on tools are the basic controls for a multistep flow.
